ranking.rationale: Commute mode is the most directly and stably linked to travel time across states: walking, transit, driving, biking, and working from home imply very different commute durations regardless of geography. It offers strong signal for acstraveltime while being less domain-leaky than explicit location features like state or PUMA.

Occupation adds strong, broadly state-stable signal for commute time beyond journey-to-work mode, since job type systematically relates to typical work locations, schedules, and travel patterns across states. It is more semantically tied to commuting than demographics like age or education, while avoiding direct geographic leakage from state or PUMA variables.

Age adds broad, state-stable signal for commute time beyond journey-to-work mode and occupation: workers at different life stages systematically sort into jobs, schedules, residential locations, and household constraints that affect travel time across states. It is less likely than geography, race, or citizenship variables to encode brittle state-specific artifacts, and more directly relevant for employed adults than child/family variables.

Education strongly and stably predicts commute time beyond age, occupation, and journey-to-work mode because it shapes job type, work location, schedule flexibility, and residential sorting in ways that generalize across states. It is less geographically brittle than PUMA/ST/POWPUMA and less shortcut-prone than race or sex, while being far more relevant for workers than child- or household-specific variables.

Income-to-poverty ratio adds broadly state-stable signal for commute time beyond age, education, occupation, and commute mode: higher resources are consistently linked to residential/job location choices and car access that affect travel time. It is less directly geographic than PUMA/ST/POWPUMA and less likely than race, sex, or citizenship to act mainly as a demographic shortcut or state-specific artifact.

Disability status adds broadly state-invariant signal for commute/travel time through labor-force attachment, commuting constraints, and work intensity, while being less likely than geography, race, sex, or migration variables to act mainly as a brittle cross-state shortcut given JWTR, OCCP, age, education, and poverty already selected.

Recent mobility status adds broadly state-invariant signal for commute time because movers, especially recent cross-area movers, are more likely to have unstable or atypical commute patterns beyond what job type, travel mode, age, education, poverty, and disability already capture. It is less directly geographic-leaking than state/PUMA/workplace identifiers and less shortcut-prone than race or sex.

Citizenship status adds plausible, state-transferable signal for commute time through labor-market attachment, job sorting, and commuting constraints, while being less directly geographic and less likely than race/sex/marital or household-relationship variables to act mainly as demographic shortcuts once age, education, poverty, occupation, migration, disability, and journey-to-work mode are already included.

Marital status adds broadly stable signal for commute time through household structure and life stage beyond age, education, occupation, and income, while being less geography-specific and less likely to act as a brittle shortcut than race or location identifiers; other remaining options are either weak for this worker-focused task or strongly encode domain geography.

Sex can add modest but real signal for commute time through broadly stable labor-force participation, occupation mix, and commuting-pattern differences that persist across states, while being less geographically brittle than PUMA/ST/POWPUMA and less likely than race or household-structure variables to act mainly as state-specific demographic shortcuts. Other remaining features are either weak for likely workers in this task or heavily encode geography.

Relationship to householder adds household-role and life-stage structure that can still affect commute patterns beyond age, marital status, sex, and income, while remaining more semantically stable across states than race or geographic identifiers. It is also broadly applicable to adults in the travel-time task, unlike parental employment status.

Race can add some residual, broadly portable signal for commute-time patterns through structural differences in residential location, job access, and mode choice that may persist across states, while being less directly geographic and less domain-leaking than PUMA, ST, or POWPUMA. ESP is mostly irrelevant for the adult worker population in acstraveltime, so RAC1P has the largest remaining stable marginal value.

Among the remaining options, this is the only non-geographic variable and thus least likely to leak state or local domain identity. It may add modest stable signal through household structure and parental work constraints, especially for younger commuters, whereas PUMA, ST, and POWPUMA are strong geography proxies that would likely hurt out-of-distribution generalization.

Among the remaining options, workplace PUMA adds the most direct signal for commute time because travel duration depends strongly on where the job is located relative to residence and transport networks. It is still geographically brittle and should be penalized, but it is less purely a domain label than state or home PUMA and offers the largest remaining marginal predictive value after commute mode, occupation, age, education, income, and migration are already included.

PUMA is still highly geography-specific and brittle across states, but it can add some residual within-state local commuting-context signal beyond occupation, travel mode, migration, and POWPUMA. ST mostly encodes the domain itself and is least likely to provide stable out-of-distribution value.

Only remaining candidate. However, its stable marginal value is low because state directly encodes the OOD domain and mainly captures geography- and policy-specific commute patterns rather than broadly transferable individual-level predictors; much of its signal is also redundant with already selected geographic features.

llm_calls.content: {"selected_feature_id":4,"rationale":"Disability status adds broadly state-invariant signal for commute/travel time through labor-force attachment, commuting constraints, and work intensity, while being less likely than geography, race, sex, or migration variables to act mainly as a brittle cross-state shortcut given JWTR, OCCP, age, education, and poverty already selected."}

{"selected_feature_id":6,"rationale":"Recent mobility status adds broadly state-invariant signal for commute time because movers, especially recent cross-area movers, are more likely to have unstable or atypical commute patterns beyond what job type, travel mode, age, education, poverty, and disability already capture. It is less directly geographic-leaking than state/PUMA/workplace identifiers and less shortcut-prone than race or sex."}

{"selected_feature_id":11,"rationale":"Citizenship status adds plausible, state-transferable signal for commute time through labor-market attachment, job sorting, and commuting constraints, while being less directly geographic and less likely than race/sex/marital or household-relationship variables to act mainly as demographic shortcuts once age, education, poverty, occupation, migration, disability, and journey-to-work mode are already included."}

{"selected_feature_id":2,"rationale":"Marital status adds broadly stable signal for commute time through household structure and life stage beyond age, education, occupation, and income, while being less geography-specific and less likely to act as a brittle shortcut than race or location identifiers; other remaining options are either weak for this worker-focused task or strongly encode domain geography."}

{"selected_feature_id":3,"rationale":"Sex can add modest but real signal for commute time through broadly stable labor-force participation, occupation mix, and commuting-pattern differences that persist across states, while being less geographically brittle than PUMA/ST/POWPUMA and less likely than race or household-structure variables to act mainly as state-specific demographic shortcuts. Other remaining features are either weak for likely workers in this task or heavily encode geography."}

{"selected_feature_id":7,"rationale":"Relationship to householder adds household-role and life-stage structure that can still affect commute patterns beyond age, marital status, sex, and income, while remaining more semantically stable across states than race or geographic identifiers. It is also broadly applicable to adults in the travel-time task, unlike parental employment status."}

{"selected_feature_id":8,"rationale":"Race can add some residual, broadly portable signal for commute-time patterns through structural differences in residential location, job access, and mode choice that may persist across states, while being less directly geographic and less domain-leaking than PUMA, ST, or POWPUMA. ESP is mostly irrelevant for the adult worker population in acstraveltime, so RAC1P has the largest remaining stable marginal value."}

{"selected_feature_id":5,"rationale":"Among the remaining options, this is the only non-geographic variable and thus least likely to leak state or local domain identity. It may add modest stable signal through household structure and parental work constraints, especially for younger commuters, whereas PUMA, ST, and POWPUMA are strong geography proxies that would likely hurt out-of-distribution generalization."}

{"selected_feature_id":14,"rationale":"Among the remaining options, workplace PUMA adds the most direct signal for commute time because travel duration depends strongly on where the job is located relative to residence and transport networks. It is still geographically brittle and should be penalized, but it is less purely a domain label than state or home PUMA and offers the largest remaining marginal predictive value after commute mode, occupation, age, education, income, and migration are already included."}

{"selected_feature_id":9,"rationale":"PUMA is still highly geography-specific and brittle across states, but it can add some residual within-state local commuting-context signal beyond occupation, travel mode, migration, and POWPUMA. ST mostly encodes the domain itself and is least likely to provide stable out-of-distribution value."}

{"selected_feature_id":10,"rationale":"Only remaining candidate. However, its stable marginal value is low because state directly encodes the OOD domain and mainly captures geography- and policy-specific commute patterns rather than broadly transferable individual-level predictors; much of its signal is also redundant with already selected geographic features."}
